venues.name: Rosewood Hong Kong
venues.note: The best hotel in the world, a vertical estate on the Kowloon waterfront, with the whole harbour at its feet.

venues.name: The Upper House
venues.note: A serene, art-filled sanctuary above the city, the quietest luxury in Hong Kong.

venues.name: Mandarin Oriental, Hong Kong
venues.note: The grande dame of Central since 1963, the address the city measures itself against.

venues.name: The Peninsula Hong Kong
venues.note: The grand old lady of the Far East, colonnaded, colonial and utterly iconic since 1928.
credentials: The World's 50 Best Hotels 2025 (No. 54, extended list)

venues.name: Four Seasons Hotel Hong Kong
venues.note: The surest hands in the city, above the harbour, service you never have to think about.
credentials: The World's 50 Best Hotels 2025 (No. 84, extended list)

venues.name: The Ritz-Carlton, Hong Kong
venues.note: The world's highest hotel, floors 102 to 118 of the ICC tower, with clouds below the window.

venues.name: The St. Regis Hong Kong
venues.note: A jewel-box house of just 129 rooms, the most personal of the city's grand hotels, with butler service throughout.

venues.name: Regent Hong Kong
venues.note: The reborn waterfront legend, floor-to-ceiling harbour glass and the finest island view in the city.

venues.name: Mandarin Oriental The Landmark, Hong Kong
venues.note: A discreet, design-led hideaway above the Landmark's luxury boutiques, pure Central, no harbour, all calm.

venues.name: The Murray, Hong Kong, a Niccolo Hotel
venues.note: A 1960s modernist landmark reborn, soaring arched windows and a garden setting rare in Central.

venues.name: Grand Hyatt Hong Kong
venues.note: A grand Art Deco house on the harbour, with one of the city's great outdoor pools and gardens.

venues.name: Island Shangri-La, Hong Kong
venues.note: Old-world grandeur above Pacific Place, chandeliers, a 16-storey mural, and Petrus high in the sky.

venues.name: Kowloon Shangri-La
venues.note: A warm, established harbourside house on the Kowloon side, grand, generous, and reliably excellent.

venues.name: W Hong Kong
venues.note: A high-energy design tower sharing the ICC with the Ritz-Carlton, the rooftop pool is the highest in the city.

venues.name: Hotel ICON
venues.note: A design-forward urban retreat with a vertical garden wall and a genuinely local Hong Kong soul.

venues.name: Conrad Hong Kong
venues.note: A polished, high-floor house above Pacific Place, dependable, central, and quietly grand.

venues.name: JW Marriott Hotel Hong Kong
venues.note: A capable, comfortable Pacific Place tower, big, well-run, and easy for business or family.

venues.name: The Langham, Hong Kong
venues.note: A refined European-style house in the heart of Kowloon's shopping and dining quarter.

venues.name: The Royal Garden
venues.note: A serene atrium-garden hotel on the Kowloon side, quietly excellent, and a local secret.

venues.name: Marco Polo Hongkong Hotel
venues.note: A dependable harbourfront address built into Harbour City, shopping, ferries and the Star Ferry at the door.

venues.name: The Peninsula Hong Kong, Peninsula Suite
venues.note: Two floors, a private terrace and the harbour laid out below, the grandest suite on the Kowloon side.

venues.name: Amber
venues.note: Richard Ekkebus's dairy-free, produce-led French, newly promoted to three stars after seventeen years.

venues.name: 8½ Otto e Mezzo BOMBANA
venues.note: Umberto Bombana's grand Italian, the only three-star Italian restaurant outside Italy.

venues.name: Caprice
venues.note: French haute cuisine and a legendary cheese trolley, high over the harbour.

venues.name: Forum
venues.note: Chef Yeung Koon Yat's temple to abalone, the most revered Cantonese kitchen in the city.

venues.name: Sushi Shikon
venues.note: An Edomae omakase of the very highest order, the fish flown from Tokyo daily.

venues.name: T'ang Court
venues.note: Refined, classical Cantonese in a hushed silk-lined room, three stars, decades in the making.

venues.name: Ta Vie
venues.note: Chef Hideaki Sato's 'travel through life', French technique, Japanese soul, tiny and exact.

venues.name: WING
venues.note: Vicky Cheng's contemporary Chinese, the second-highest a Hong Kong restaurant has ever placed in the world.

venues.name: The Chairman
venues.note: Old Hong Kong Cantonese with a conscience, free-range, local, seasonal, and quietly world-beating.

venues.name: Arbor
venues.note: A precise, seasonal Franco-Japanese tasting menu in a serene Central room.

venues.name: Lung King Heen
venues.note: The first Chinese restaurant in the world to hold three stars, now two, still peerless Cantonese.

venues.name: Lai Ching Heen
venues.note: Classical Cantonese with jade tableware and a full-frontal harbour view.

venues.name: L'Envol
venues.note: Delicate, luminous French cooking in a light-filled St. Regis room.

venues.name: Bo Innovation
venues.note: Alvin Leung's 'X-treme Chinese', provocative, technical, unlike anywhere else.

venues.name: Octavium
venues.note: An intimate, members'-club-feel Italian from the Bombana school, precise and grown-up.

venues.name: Rùn
venues.note: Refined Sichuan and Cantonese in a jewel-box setting, heat handled with real finesse.

venues.name: TATE Dining Room
venues.note: Vicky Lau's 'edible poetry', a French-Chinese ode to Hong Kong, told in delicate courses.

venues.name: Tin Lung Heen
venues.note: Grand Cantonese on the 102nd floor, the finest dim sum in the sky.

venues.name: Ying Jee Club
venues.note: Polished, classical Cantonese from a celebrated master, quietly one of Central's best.

venues.name: Neighborhood
venues.note: David Lai's market-driven European bistro cooking, no menu, endless charm, always full.

venues.name: MONO
venues.note: Ricardo Chaneton's Latin-American-accented cooking, the flavours of his roots, refined.

venues.name: Estro
venues.note: Antimo Merone's ode to Campania, soulful, personal southern-Italian cooking.

venues.name: Andō
venues.note: Agustin Balbi's Argentine-Spanish-Japanese kitchen, a deeply personal tasting menu.

venues.name: VEA
venues.note: Vicky Cheng's original, a Chinese-French counter of great craft, above his flagship WING.

venues.name: Feuille
venues.note: David Toutain protégé's plant-forward, nature-led cooking, green, precise and quietly radical.

venues.name: Xin Rong Ji
venues.note: The Beijing sensation's Hong Kong outpost, pristine Taizhou seafood and yellow croaker.

venues.name: Testina
venues.note: Milanese cooking done with real heart, nose-to-tail Italian, and a Bib to prove the value.

venues.name: New Punjab Club
venues.note: The first Punjabi restaurant in the world to hold a Michelin star, tandoor-fired and proudly Indian.

venues.name: CHAAT
venues.note: Chef Manav Tuli's modern Indian inside the world's best hotel, bright, spiced, beautifully judged.

venues.name: Louise
venues.note: Julien Royer's French cooking in a restored heritage house, classical, warm, immaculate.

venues.name: Roganic
venues.note: Simon Rogan's farm-to-table ethos, translated to Hong Kong, hyper-seasonal and green.

venues.name: Petrus
venues.note: Grand French dining on the 56th floor, chandeliers, a great wine list, and the harbour beyond.

venues.name: Gaddi's
venues.note: The most storied French dining room in Asia, grand, gilded, and going strong since 1953.

venues.name: Cristal Room by Anne-Sophie Pic
venues.note: Anne-Sophie Pic's delicate, aromatic French in a Baccarat-crystal setting overlooking the harbour.

venues.name: Man Wah
venues.note: Refined Cantonese on the 25th floor of the grande dame, a jewel-box of a dining room.

venues.name: Spring Moon
venues.note: Art Deco Cantonese in the Peninsula, dim sum, roast goose and a famous tea menu.

venues.name: Shang Palace
venues.note: Sumptuous, red-and-gold classical Cantonese, a grand-hotel banquet done properly.

venues.name: Yardbird
venues.note: The yakitori izakaya that changed how Hong Kong eats out, every part of the bird, no reservations.

venues.name: Beefbar
venues.note: A glamorous temple to the world's finest beef, in a heritage former bank hall.

venues.name: BELON
venues.note: A neo-Parisian bistro of real soul, the roast chicken has a devoted following.

venues.name: Kam's Roast Goose
venues.note: A one-star roast-goose shop from the Yung Kee dynasty, crisp skin, no ceremony, always a queue.

venues.name: Yat Lok
venues.note: A tiny, tiled roast-goose canteen with a Michelin star, the roast goose over rice is the reason.

venues.name: Ho Hung Kee
venues.note: A congee-and-noodle institution since the 1940s, wonton noodles that earned a star.

venues.name: Ho Lee Fook
venues.note: Modern Cantonese comfort food with swagger, the wagyu short rib and roast goose bring the crowds.

venues.name: Carbone
venues.note: The New York Italian-American theatre, tableside caesar, veal parm, and a room that never quietens.

venues.name: Involtini
venues.note: Honest, generous Sicilian home cooking in a warm neighbourhood room.

venues.name: Chesa
venues.note: The Peninsula's tiny Swiss chalet, fondue and raclette, unchanged and beloved for decades.

venues.name: Luk Yu Tea House
venues.note: A 1930s Cantonese tea house frozen in time, trolley dim sum, teak booths, living history.

venues.name: One Harbour Road
venues.note: Refined Cantonese in a 1930s-Shanghai-tai-pan-mansion setting, overlooking the harbour.

venues.name: Mandarin Grill + Bar
venues.note: The grande dame's grill, a Terence Conran room, a seafood bar, and old-Hong-Kong glamour.

venues.name: Fook Lam Moon
venues.note: The 'tycoons' canteen', old-money Cantonese banqueting, abalone and roast suckling pig.

venues.name: Duddell's
venues.note: An art-filled Cantonese salon with a garden terrace, dim sum among rotating exhibitions.

venues.name: Summer Palace
venues.note: Opulent, classical Cantonese in a grand-hotel room, a benchmark for the old-school banquet.

venues.name: Sun Tung Lok
venues.note: A long-revered name for abalone, seafood and refined Cantonese classics.

venues.name: Hansik Goo
venues.note: A modern Korean 'hansik' tasting menu of real refinement, the best Korean fine dining in town.

venues.name: Victoria Peak & the Peak Tram
venues.note: Ride Asia's oldest funicular (1888) up the mountainside, then walk the flat 3.5km Peak Circle Walk for the postcard sweep over the harbour and skyscraper canyon. Come at dusk to catch the towers switch on; a private car and skip-the-line tram booking spares the family the notorious queue.

venues.name: Star Ferry across Victoria Harbour
venues.note: The green-and-white ferries have crossed the harbour since 1888 and remain the cheapest, most cinematic ride in the city. Sit on the open upper deck between Tsim Sha Tsui and Central at sunset with the whole skyline gliding past on both sides.

venues.name: A Symphony of Lights
venues.note: Every night at 8pm, around 40 buildings on both sides of the harbour perform a synchronised light-and-laser show. Watch from the Tsim Sha Tsui promenade or, for a private angle, book a junk cruise so the family sees it from the water.
credentials: Guinness World Record, largest permanent light and sound show

venues.name: Tsim Sha Tsui Promenade & Avenue of Stars
venues.note: A breezy harbour-front walk with the finest head-on view of Hong Kong Island's skyline, past the Bruce Lee statue and handprints of Cantonese cinema legends. Ends near the Clock Tower, a lone relic of the old Kowloon railway terminus.

venues.name: M+ Museum
venues.note: Herzog & de Meuron's vast museum of 20th- and 21st-century visual culture, design, moving image, architecture and Asian contemporary art, with a giant LED facade facing the harbour. One of the largest museums of modern visual culture in the world; the rooftop and harbour-view galleries reward an unhurried afternoon.

venues.name: Hong Kong Palace Museum
venues.note: A striking golden building showing treasures on rotating loan from Beijing's Forbidden City, imperial jade, ceramics, paintings and court life, curated for a modern audience. Pairs naturally with M+ next door for a full culture day.

venues.name: Tai Kwun, Centre for Heritage & Arts
venues.note: The beautifully restored former Central Police Station, Magistracy and Victoria Prison, now a compound of galleries, courtyards, boutiques and restaurants. Wander the granite cells and colonial verandahs, then eat well; it is one of the city's most discreet, unhurried spots.
credentials: UNESCO Asia-Pacific Award of Excellence for Cultural Heritage Conservation, 2019

venues.name: Man Mo Temple
venues.note: Hong Kong's most atmospheric temple, dedicated to the gods of literature and war, its dim hall hazed with enormous hanging incense coils. A short, calm stop on the way up steep Ladder Street and Hollywood Road's antique galleries.

venues.name: Tian Tan Buddha (Big Buddha) & Po Lin Monastery
venues.note: Climb 268 steps to the world's largest outdoor seated bronze Buddha, serene above the Lantau hills, beside the century-old Po Lin Monastery. The monastery's famous vegetarian canteen is fully veg and Jain-friendly-adjacent, a rare, easy meal for plant-based families.
credentials: World's largest outdoor seated bronze Buddha

venues.name: Ngong Ping 360 Cable Car
venues.note: A 25-minute glass-cabin glide over the sea, the airport and North Lantau's green ridges to Ngong Ping village and the Big Buddha. Splurge on a Crystal Cabin with a glass floor; the panorama is the reason to come even before the Buddha.

venues.name: Dragon's Back Trail
venues.area: Shek O / Southern District, Hong Kong Island
venues.note: The city's most loved ridge hike, a gentle, undulating spine with sweeping views over Shek O, Tai Long Wan and the South China Sea, ending at a beach. Around 8km and family-doable; a driver can meet you at the Big Wave Bay end.
credentials: Named Asia's Best Urban Hiking Trail by TIME

venues.name: Hong Kong UNESCO Global Geopark
venues.note: Extraordinary hexagonal volcanic rock columns and sea-carved sedimentary formations across the eastern New Territories, best seen by boat from Sai Kung. Charter a private sampan or junk to reach the sea arches and coves in comfort.

venues.name: Sai Kung & the East Country Parks
venues.note: A relaxed fishing town with a live seafood harbour-front, gateway to Hong Kong's cleanest beaches and the MacLehose Trail. Hire a boat to Tai Long Wan's white-sand bays, the closest thing the city has to a private island day.

venues.name: Wong Tai Sin Temple
venues.note: A vivid, busy Taoist temple where worshippers shake fortune sticks and consult soothsayers, surrounded by a serene Good Wish Garden and koi ponds. Said to 'make every wish come true', a colourful, welcoming stop for multi-generational visitors.

venues.name: Chi Lin Nunnery & Nan Lian Garden
venues.note: A vast Tang-dynasty-style wooden monastery built without a single nail, beside a meticulously landscaped classical garden with a golden pavilion and lotus ponds. Utterly tranquil, free, and home to a refined vegetarian restaurant behind a waterfall.

venues.name: Temple Street Night Market
venues.note: Kowloon's classic after-dark bazaar of stalls, fortune-tellers, Cantonese opera singers and open-air dai pai dong seafood. Loud, theatrical and full of old-Hong-Kong character; go early evening with the family before the crowds thicken.

venues.name: Sham Shui Po
venues.note: The city's grittiest, most authentic district, fabric and bead streets, electronics arcades, and some of Hong Kong's best cheap eats and third-wave coffee. A design-lover's treasure hunt; go with a guide to find the Michelin-listed street food.

venues.name: Hollywood Road & Cat Street antiques
venues.note: Hong Kong's antiques spine, lined with serious dealers in Ming ceramics, jade and Chinese furniture, plus the flea-market bric-a-brac of Cat Street (Upper Lascar Row). The place for collectors to source with provenance and arrange discreet shipping home.

venues.name: PMQ
venues.note: A former police married-quarters block reborn as a hive of independent Hong Kong designers, jewellers and craft studios. Ideal for finding one-of-a-kind gifts and meeting the makers, with a quiet courtyard cafe to regroup.

venues.name: Central–Mid-Levels Escalator & SoHo
venues.note: Ride the world's longest outdoor covered escalator system uphill through the layered lanes of SoHo and NoHo, hopping off for galleries, wine bars and global restaurants. The easiest way to graze Central's dense dining scene on foot.
credentials: World's longest outdoor covered escalator system

venues.name: Ding Ding, Hong Kong Tramways
venues.note: Board a double-decker tram, running since 1904, and ride the whole north shore from Kennedy Town to Shau Kei Wan for the price of a coffee. Grab the front upper-deck seat for a slow, open-window film reel of street life.
credentials: World's largest fleet of double-decker trams in service

venues.name: Lamma Island
venues.note: A car-free island of green hills, a gentle family walk between Yung Shue Wan and Sok Kwu Wan, and waterfront seafood restaurants at the end. A slow, restorative half-day escape barely 30 minutes by ferry from Central.

venues.name: Cheung Chau Island
venues.note: A dumbbell-shaped fishing island with a bustling harbour, seafood shacks, a small beach and pirate-cave legends, plus the springtime Bun Festival. Rent bikes and let children roam the car-free lanes; utterly unhurried.

venues.name: Tai O fishing village
venues.note: A photogenic stilt-house village on Lantau's west coast, where Tanka fishing families live over the water and shops sell dried seafood and shrimp paste. Take a short boat ride to spot pink dolphins, then stay across the water at the heritage Tai O Heritage Hotel.

venues.name: Ping Shan Heritage Trail
venues.note: Hong Kong's first heritage trail winds through 900 years of Tang-clan history, ancestral halls, a study hall and the territory's only ancient pagoda, the Tsui Sing Lau. A quiet window into pre-colonial walled-village life, far from the tourist crush.

venues.name: Hong Kong Museum of History
venues.note: The excellent 'Hong Kong Story' walk-through, from prehistoric coastline to fishing villages, opium wars and the modern metropolis, with life-size street recreations. The single best hour for grounding the family in how this city came to be.

venues.name: Hong Kong Museum of Art
venues.note: A refreshed, harbour-facing museum of Chinese antiquities, ink painting, and the superb Chih Lo Lou classical Chinese art collection. Calm, air-conditioned galleries with the skyline framed through the windows.

venues.name: Flagstaff House Museum of Tea Ware
venues.note: Hong Kong's oldest surviving colonial building, now a jewel-box museum of Chinese tea culture and Yixing teapots inside leafy Hong Kong Park. Combine with the park's aviary and conservatory for an easy, shaded family morning.
credentials: Declared Monument, oldest surviving Western-style building in Hong Kong

venues.name: Ocean Park
venues.note: A cliffside marine-and-thrills park spread over a headland, linked by cable car and funicular, with pandas, an enormous aquarium and roller coasters over the sea. A classic full family day for younger children and teens alike.

venues.name: Hong Kong Disneyland
venues.note: A compact, well-run Disney park with the world's only Mystic Manor and a growing 'World of Frozen' land. Stay at a park hotel and use a VIP tour host so multi-generational groups skip the queues entirely.

venues.name: Aberdeen Harbour & sampan ride
venues.note: Once a floating fishing community, still crowded with junks and yachts; take a traditional sampan among the boats for a glimpse of old maritime Hong Kong. A short, atmospheric ride that grandparents especially enjoy.

venues.name: Stanley & Stanley Market
venues.note: A relaxed seaside town on the island's south coast with a lanes-and-stalls market, breezy waterfront restaurants and the transplanted colonial Murray House. A soft, sunny counterpoint to the city's density.

venues.name: Repulse Bay & the Southern beaches
venues.note: The island's most fashionable crescent of sand, backed by the wave-shaped Repulse Bay building and the kitsch-but-fun Tin Hau shrine at its eastern end. Genteel, family-safe swimming with beach-club lunching nearby.

venues.name: Kowloon Walled City Park
venues.note: A serene Jiangnan-style garden built on the site of the infamous, now-demolished Walled City, the densest place on earth, with a small museum explaining its lawless past. A quiet, curious stop after nearby Kowloon City's Thai and Chiu Chow food.

venues.name: Ten Thousand Buddhas Monastery
venues.note: Climb a hillside path flanked by hundreds of individually posed, life-size golden arhat statues to a hall lined with roughly 13,000 small Buddha figures. Offbeat, uncrowded and genuinely memorable; wear good shoes for the steps.

venues.name: Sik Sik Yuen & the Sha Tin racecourse experience
venues.note: Hong Kong's grand racecourse hosts world-class Wednesday-night and weekend meets in an electric, food-filled atmosphere. Book a members' box or Chinese-cuisine viewing suite for a discreet, catered evening at the heart of the city's oldest passion.

venues.name: Lan Kwai Fong & Central nightlife
venues.note: The compact hillside of bars, izakayas and rooftops that empties the offices after dark, ringed by SoHo's more grown-up drinking dens. For a refined evening, aim instead at the harbour-view speakeasies and hotel bars just downhill.

venues.name: Ozone Bar, The Ritz-Carlton
venues.note: One of the world's highest bars, on the 118th floor of the ICC tower, with the entire harbour and Hong Kong Island laid out below. A memorable sundowner; reserve a window table well ahead.
credentials: Among the world's highest rooftop bars

venues.name: Sky100 Observation Deck
venues.note: A 360-degree indoor observation deck on the 100th floor of Hong Kong's tallest building, the best all-weather panorama when the Peak is cloud-covered. Easy and step-free, good for less mobile family members.

venues.name: Cantonese dim sum & tea houses
venues.note: Yum cha, the ritual of tea and small plates, is Hong Kong's culinary soul, from trolley-service old-timers to Michelin-starred rooms. Ask an advisor to book a private room and pre-arrange vegetarian and Jain-suitable dishes so nothing is a compromise.

venues.name: Choi Hung Estate & Instagram Hong Kong
venues.note: The rainbow-painted 1960s public-housing estate with its basketball courts has become an icon of graphic Hong Kong. One of a cluster of striking modernist estates (with Montane Mansion's 'Monster Building') that photographers seek out.

venues.name: Hong Kong Wetland Park
venues.note: A large, well-designed reserve of mangroves, mudflats and boardwalks alive with migratory birds, mudskippers and a resident crocodile. Buggy-friendly and shaded, a genuinely restful nature morning for families with small children.

venues.name: Peak-to-Aberdeen & Pok Fu Lam heritage walk
venues.note: Quiet country trails link the Peak down through Pok Fu Lam past a colonial dairy-farm village and reservoir to the coast. A gentler alternative to Dragon's Back, ending near the seafood of Aberdeen.

venues.name: Junk cruise on Victoria Harbour
venues.note: Charter a red-sailed junk or a private motor yacht to drift through the harbour at golden hour, drinks in hand, the skyline turning on around you. The city's signature private experience, book the whole boat for the family.

venues.name: Macau day trip, Historic Centre
venues.note: An hour by fast ferry to a Portuguese-Chinese old town of pastel churches, the Ruins of St Paul's, cobbled Senado Square and A-Ma Temple, plus egg tarts and world-class casino resorts. Skip the gaming floors for a private heritage-and-dining day, or the reverse.
credentials: UNESCO World Heritage Site, Historic Centre of Macao

venues.name: Bar Leone
venues.note: Lorenzo Antinori's 'popular Roman bar', unfussy Italian aperitivi, done so well it became the finest bar on earth.

venues.name: Coa
venues.note: Jay Khan's temple to agave, 200-plus tequilas and mezcals, and hospitality that redefined the Asian bar.
credentials: Asia's 50 Best Bars, No. 1 three years running (2021–2023)

venues.name: Argo
venues.note: The Four Seasons' flagship bar, a sustainability-led cocktail programme and rare spirits, poured with hotel-grade polish.

venues.name: Penicillin
venues.note: The world's first closed-loop sustainable bar, house ferments, zero waste, and a serious cocktail behind the ethic.

venues.name: The Old Man
venues.note: A Hemingway-inspired snug of literary cocktails, once the best bar in Asia, and still a rite of passage.

venues.name: Quinary
venues.note: Antonio Lai's laboratory, the birthplace of molecular mixology in Hong Kong, all foams, mists and multisensory theatre.
credentials: Long-running The World's 50 Best Bars listee

venues.name: DarkSide
venues.note: A velvet-and-Murano jazz parlour of dark spirits, cigars and live music, the most glamorous late night on the Kowloon side.
credentials: Asia's 50 Best Bars, listed four years running

venues.name: Ozone
venues.note: The world's highest bar, on the 118th floor of the ICC, cocktails in the clouds, with the whole harbour far below.

venues.name: Aqua
venues.note: A double-height glass room and terrace on the 30th floor of One Peking, the classic full-frontal skyline view with a drink in hand.

venues.name: The Aubrey
venues.note: A theatrical Japanese-inspired izakaya-bar in the grande dame, jewel-box interiors and one of the city's best cocktail lists.

venues.name: The Savory Project
venues.note: A tiny bar built entirely on savoury, umami-driven cocktails, the most inventive drinking in the city right now.

venues.name: Sevva
venues.note: Bonnae Gokson's rooftop terrace atop Prince's Building, wrapped around the towers of Central, glamorous and enduring.

venues.name: The Envoy
venues.note: A polished terrace bar above Stanley Street with a classic-cocktail pedigree, old-Hong-Kong elegance, done properly.

venues.name: Lobby Lounge & Felix, The Peninsula
venues.note: A drink at the grande dame of Kowloon, the Lobby by day, Philippe Starck's 28th-floor Felix by night, harbour spread below.

venues.name: Lan Kwai Fong
venues.note: The city's original nightlife quarter, a hillside of bars and clubs that spills into the street. Loud, packed, unmissable once.
